options.text: The splitting of a large atomic nucleus into smaller nuclei
options.feedback: Correct -- fission breaks a heavy nucleus (like uranium) apart, releasing energy.

options.text: The joining of two small nuclei into one larger nucleus
options.feedback: That describes fusion, the opposite process of fission.

options.text: The process of an atom losing an electron
options.feedback: That describes ionization, a chemical-level process, not nuclear fission.

options.text: The process of a substance melting
options.feedback: Melting is a physical state change, unrelated to nuclear fission.

medium.text: What is nuclear fusion, and where does it occur naturally on a massive scale?

options.text: The joining of small nuclei into a larger one, occurring naturally in stars like the Sun
options.feedback: Correct -- fusion of hydrogen into helium is the process powering the Sun and other stars.

options.text: The splitting of large nuclei, occurring naturally in ordinary rocks
options.feedback: This describes fission, not fusion, and fission isn't a large-scale natural process in ordinary rocks.

options.text: The joining of nuclei, occurring naturally in ice
options.feedback: Fusion requires extreme temperatures and pressures found in stars, not conditions found in ordinary ice.

options.text: A process that only happens in laboratories, never in nature
options.feedback: Fusion is actually the dominant natural energy source powering stars throughout the universe.

hard.text: Both fission and fusion release large amounts of energy, but why is fusion generally considered a potentially cleaner energy source than fission for power generation?

options.text: Fusion typically produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission
options.feedback: Correct -- fission byproducts often remain radioactive for a very long time, whereas fusion's primary products are generally much less hazardous long-term.

options.text: Fusion doesn't release any energy at all
options.feedback: Fusion actually releases a tremendous amount of energy, even more per reaction than typical fission reactions.

options.text: Fission doesn't require any radioactive material to begin with
options.feedback: Fission specifically requires radioactive heavy elements like uranium, unlike this claim.

options.text: Fusion reactions are easier to control and have already been fully commercialized for decades
options.feedback: Fusion is actually notoriously difficult to sustain and control, and commercial fusion power isn't yet fully achieved -- this isn't the reason it's considered cleaner.

easy.hard: This process breaks a heavy atomic nucleus apart into lighter pieces, releasing energy in the process.
easy.medium: This is when a large atomic nucleus gets split into smaller pieces.
easy.easy: This is when a big atomic nucleus splits into smaller pieces.

medium.hard: Under extreme temperature and pressure conditions found in stellar cores, light nuclei can overcome repulsion to combine into heavier ones.
medium.medium: Under the extreme heat and pressure inside stars, small atomic nuclei can smash together and combine.
medium.easy: Inside stars, small atomic nuclei get smashed together under extreme heat and pressure.

hard.hard: Fission of heavy elements tends to produce unstable daughter isotopes that remain radioactive for extended periods, while fusion's typical byproducts (like helium) are much less hazardous in comparison.
hard.medium: The leftover material from splitting atoms tends to stay dangerously radioactive for a very long time, unlike what's left over from fusing atoms together.
hard.easy: The leftover material from splitting atoms stays dangerous for a really long time, unlike the leftovers from fusing atoms.

easy.text: What force keeps planets orbiting around the Sun?

options.text: Gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- the Sun's gravitational pull continuously bends the planets' paths into orbits.

options.text: Magnetism
options.feedback: Magnetism isn't the force responsible for planetary orbits -- gravity is.

options.text: Friction
options.feedback: Friction requires surfaces rubbing together, which doesn't apply to planets orbiting in the vacuum of space.

options.text: Air pressure
options.feedback: There's essentially no air in space to exert pressure -- gravity alone keeps planets in orbit.

medium.text: Why don't orbiting planets simply fall straight into the Sun, given that gravity is constantly pulling them inward?

options.text: Their forward (sideways) velocity continuously carries them past the Sun, resulting in a curved orbital path instead of a straight fall
options.feedback: Correct -- orbit is essentially a perpetual 'falling' that's balanced by enough sideways motion to keep missing the object being orbited.

options.text: The Sun's gravity actually pushes planets away, not pulls them in
options.feedback: Gravity is fundamentally an attractive force, always pulling objects together, not pushing them apart.

options.text: There is no real gravitational force acting on the planets
options.feedback: Gravity is very much acting on the planets -- it's precisely what curves their paths into orbits.

options.text: Planets are too heavy for gravity to have any effect
options.feedback: Gravity's effect actually scales with mass in a way that keeps working regardless of how large or small the orbiting object is.

hard.text: Why do planets farther from the Sun (like Neptune) take much longer to complete one orbit than planets closer to the Sun (like Mercury)?

options.text: Farther planets travel a much larger orbital distance AND experience weaker gravitational pull, both of which result in slower orbital speeds and longer periods
options.feedback: Correct -- both the greater distance to travel and the Sun's weaker gravitational influence at that distance combine to significantly lengthen the orbital period.

options.text: Farther planets are simply much heavier than closer ones
options.feedback: Planet mass isn't the primary factor determining orbital period -- distance from the Sun and gravitational strength at that distance are far more significant.

options.text: Farther planets have stronger gravity pulling them around faster
options.feedback: This is backwards -- gravitational pull from the Sun actually weakens with increasing distance, contributing to slower orbital motion.

options.text: There is no real difference in orbital time between near and far planets
options.feedback: There's a dramatic, well-documented difference in orbital periods based on distance from the Sun -- this isn't a myth.

easy.hard: This universal force of attraction acts between any two masses, curving their relative motion.
easy.medium: This is the invisible pulling force between any two massive objects, like the Sun and planets.
easy.easy: This is the same force that makes things fall to the ground on Earth.

medium.hard: An orbit results from a delicate balance between an object's sideways momentum and the constant inward pull of gravity, causing a continuous curved 'fall' rather than a direct collision.
medium.medium: The planet is moving sideways fast enough that as gravity pulls it in, it just keeps missing the Sun, tracing a curved path instead.
medium.easy: The planet is moving sideways fast enough that gravity just curves its path instead of pulling it straight in.

hard.hard: Kepler's laws show that both the larger circumference of the orbital path and the weaker gravitational acceleration at greater distances contribute to a longer period for outer planets.
hard.medium: Farther planets have a much longer path to travel around the Sun, and the Sun's pull on them is also weaker out there, both slowing things down.
hard.easy: Farther planets have a much longer path to travel, and the Sun's pull is weaker way out there, so it takes longer.

easy.text: What is a wheel and axle, as a simple machine?

options.text: A wheel attached to a rod (axle) that rotate together to make moving objects easier
options.feedback: Correct -- a doorknob and a steering wheel are both examples of this simple machine.

options.text: A flat surface used to slide objects up
options.feedback: That describes an inclined plane, a different type of simple machine.

options.text: A rope looped around a wheel to lift objects
options.feedback: That describes a pulley, a different type of simple machine.

options.text: A rigid bar that pivots around a fixed point
options.feedback: That describes a lever, a different type of simple machine.

medium.text: Why does turning a large steering wheel require less force than turning a small one to produce the same turning effect on the axle?

options.text: The larger wheel provides more leverage (distance from the center), increasing the mechanical advantage
options.feedback: Correct -- a bigger wheel radius means the same force applied at the edge produces more torque on the connected axle.

options.text: A larger wheel weighs less than a small one
options.feedback: Wheel size doesn't necessarily correlate with weight in this way -- the mechanical advantage comes from the larger radius, not reduced weight.

options.text: A larger wheel has no actual connection to the axle
options.feedback: The wheel and axle are mechanically connected and rotate together -- that connection is exactly how the mechanical advantage is transmitted.

options.text: There is no real difference in force needed between wheel sizes
options.feedback: Wheel size genuinely affects the mechanical advantage and the force needed to achieve the same turning effect.

hard.text: A large wheel with a radius of 20 cm is attached to a small axle with a radius of 4 cm. What is the mechanical advantage of this wheel and axle system?

options.feedback: Correct -- mechanical advantage equals the wheel's radius divided by the axle's radius: 20÷4=5.
This subtracts the radii instead of dividing them.
This adds the radii instead of dividing them.
This multiplies the radii instead of dividing them.

easy.hard: This simple machine pairs a large circular component with a smaller connected rod, rotating together as one unit.
easy.medium: Think of a doorknob -- a bigger part you turn, connected to a smaller rod inside.
easy.easy: A doorknob is a common example of this simple machine.

medium.hard: A greater radius at the point of applied force multiplies the resulting torque delivered to the connected, smaller-radius axle.
medium.medium: Applying force farther from the center (a bigger wheel) creates more turning power on the smaller axle.
medium.easy: Pushing on a bigger wheel, farther from the center, gives you more turning power.

hard.hard: Divide the radius of the larger wheel by the radius of the smaller axle to find the mechanical advantage.
hard.medium: Divide the wheel's radius by the axle's radius.

easy.text: What unit is commonly used to measure the loudness (intensity) of sound?

options.text: Decibels
options.feedback: Correct -- decibels (dB) measure sound intensity/loudness.

options.text: Meters
options.feedback: Meters measure distance or length, not sound loudness.

options.text: Kilograms
options.feedback: Kilograms measure mass, not sound loudness.

options.text: Degrees
options.feedback: Degrees typically measure temperature or angles, not sound loudness.

medium.text: What is the key difference between pitch and loudness (intensity) of a sound?

options.text: Pitch relates to frequency (how high or low a sound is), while loudness relates to intensity/amplitude (how strong the sound is)
options.feedback: Correct -- these are two distinct properties of a sound wave, describing different aspects of how we perceive it.

options.text: Pitch and loudness are exactly the same thing
options.feedback: These are genuinely distinct properties, even though both relate to characteristics of sound.

options.text: Pitch measures how loud a sound is, while loudness measures how high or low it is
options.feedback: This has the definitions swapped -- pitch is about high/low tone (frequency), loudness is about volume/intensity.

options.text: Loudness only applies to music, not everyday sounds
options.feedback: Loudness applies to any sound at all, not just music specifically.

hard.text: The decibel scale is logarithmic, meaning each 10 dB increase represents roughly a 10-fold increase in sound intensity. Why is a logarithmic scale used for measuring sound instead of a simple linear one?

options.text: Human hearing can detect an enormous range of sound intensities, and a logarithmic scale makes this vast range more manageable to represent with smaller numbers
options.feedback: Correct -- without a logarithmic scale, representing the full range of audible sound intensity would require using extremely large, unwieldy numbers.

options.text: It makes the numbers bigger and harder to understand on purpose
options.feedback: The logarithmic scale is actually meant to make an otherwise unwieldy range of numbers more manageable, not intentionally confusing.

options.text: It has nothing to do with how human ears actually perceive sound
options.feedback: The logarithmic decibel scale was specifically designed to roughly match how human ears perceive relative loudness.

options.text: Sound doesn't actually vary much in intensity, so any scale would work the same
options.feedback: Sound intensity actually varies enormously, from a whisper to a jet engine -- this vast range is exactly why a logarithmic scale is useful.

easy.hard: This unit expresses sound intensity on a scale where large jumps represent proportionally larger real-world increases.
easy.medium: This unit measures how loud a sound actually is.
easy.easy: This is the unit used to measure how loud sounds are.

medium.hard: One property relates to how frequently the sound wave oscillates; the other relates to the amount of energy/amplitude carried by the wave.
medium.medium: One property is about how high or low a sound seems; the other is about how strong or soft it seems.
medium.easy: Pitch is about how high or low a sound is; loudness is about how strong it is.

hard.hard: Since audible sound intensity spans many orders of magnitude, a logarithmic scale compresses that huge range into a much more practical and manageable set of numbers.
hard.medium: Since sounds can range from extremely quiet to extremely intense, using powers of ten keeps the numbers from getting impossibly huge.
hard.easy: Since sounds range from very quiet to super loud, this special scale keeps the numbers from getting way too big.

options.text: When light traveling within a denser medium reflects entirely off a boundary instead of passing through
options.feedback: Correct -- under the right conditions, light can be completely reflected back rather than refracting out.

options.text: When light is completely absorbed by a material
options.feedback: Absorption means the light energy is taken in, not reflected -- total internal reflection is about bouncing all the light back.

options.text: When a mirror breaks into pieces
options.feedback: This isn't related to mirror breakage -- it's an optical phenomenon involving light behavior at a boundary.

options.text: When light travels in a perfectly straight line forever
options.feedback: This isn't what total internal reflection describes -- it specifically involves light reflecting off an internal boundary.

medium.text: Total internal reflection is the key principle behind which common technology?

options.text: Fiber optic cables
options.feedback: Correct -- light bounces repeatedly inside the fiber via total internal reflection, allowing data to travel long distances with minimal loss.

options.text: Ordinary incandescent light bulbs
options.feedback: Light bulbs work by heating a filament to produce light, unrelated to total internal reflection.

options.text: Battery-powered flashlights
options.feedback: Flashlights simply emit light outward -- they don't rely on the principle of total internal reflection.

options.text: Solar panels
options.feedback: Solar panels convert light into electricity via the photovoltaic effect, unrelated to total internal reflection.

hard.text: For total internal reflection to occur, light must be traveling from a denser medium toward a less dense one, AND the angle of incidence must exceed a specific 'critical angle.' Why does this angle condition matter?

options.text: Below the critical angle, some light still refracts (exits) the boundary; only above it does ALL the light reflect back internally
options.feedback: Correct -- the critical angle marks the specific threshold beyond which refraction becomes impossible and 100% of the light reflects internally.

options.text: The critical angle has no real effect on whether light reflects or refracts
options.feedback: The critical angle is precisely the threshold that determines whether total internal reflection occurs -- it's central to the phenomenon.

options.text: Below the critical angle, light disappears completely
options.feedback: Below the critical angle, light doesn't disappear -- it partially refracts (exits) and partially reflects, rather than being fully retained inside.

options.text: The critical angle only matters for colored light, not white light
options.feedback: The critical angle concept applies generally to light behavior at a boundary, not specifically tied to color.

easy.hard: This phenomenon occurs when light striking a boundary from within a material cannot escape and bounces back entirely instead.
easy.medium: This happens when light hitting a boundary from inside a material bounces all the way back instead of escaping.
easy.easy: This is when light bounces completely back inside a material instead of escaping out.

medium.hard: This technology relies on light continuously reflecting internally along a thin, flexible strand to carry signals over long distances.
medium.medium: This thin cable carries light (and data) over long distances by bouncing the light internally along its length.
medium.easy: This thin glass or plastic cable carries light signals for things like internet data.

hard.hard: The critical angle is the specific incidence angle at which refraction becomes mathematically impossible (per Snell's Law), so beyond it, 100% of the light must reflect rather than partially exit.
hard.medium: Once the light hits at a steep enough angle, it simply can't bend out anymore and has to bounce all the way back instead.
hard.easy: Once the light hits at just the right steep angle, it can't escape anymore and bounces all the way back.
